articles.title: In 1979, a Montana electrician promised to build a statue if his wife survived cancer: Six years later, a 90-foot figure stood above Butte
articles.summary: US News: Butte electrician Bob O'Bill made a promise during his wife's battle with cancer in 1979. If Joyce recovered, he would build a statue of the Virgin Ma.
articles.body: Butte electrician Bob O'Bill made a promise during his wife's battle with cancer in 1979. If Joyce recovered, he would build a statue of the Virgin Mary in her honor. Joyce survived, and O'Bill eventually turned the small idea into a 90-foot statue on a mountain above Butte. The statue is now known as Our Lady of the Rockies, and stands on the Continental Divide's East Ridge, about 3,500 feet above Butte. According to the official Our Lady of the Rockies organization, construction began in 1979 and took six years, with residents contributing labor and helping raise money for the project.O'Bill's original plan was much smaller, since he had imagined a modest statue that could be placed near his home. The project grew after other people became involved. Engineers, welders, construction workers, and volunteers eventually worked on a structure far larger than the one O'Bill had first envisioned.A small promise became a community projectO'Bill was an electrician who had worked for the Anaconda Company and Montana Power Co. before retiring. His wife's illness gave him the original reason for the project, but the statue soon became a community effort. The Butte-Silver Bow Public Archives records the beginning of the project in December 1979. The archives state that O'Bill promised to build a shrine if his wife recovered from cancer. Joyce did recover, and the project expanded beyond the couple into a community effort involving volunteers from around Butte. The archives state that residents spent nearly six years constructing the statue, while trying to build roads and raise money for the project.The proposed statue would stand on East Ridge, high above the city. Getting construction materials to the site required roads and other infrastructure before the statue itself could be completed. The project required a lot of funding and volunteer work. O'Bill organized fundraising while other people contributed labor, equipment and technical expertise. The statue was designed by Laurien Eugene Riehl, a retired mining engineer, and Leroy Lee, a local welder, fabricated the structure. The project did not require a commercial construction company to carry out the entire job; instead, different people contributed their skills at different stages.Building a 90-foot statue on a mountainButte was dealing with a difficult period in its mining history while the construction was taking place. Copper production had declined, and major changes were taking place in the local mining industry. The statue itself was constructed away from its final position, and getting it onto the mountain required another engineering operation. The official organization says workers poured a 400-ton concrete base in September 1985. The statue was ready to be transported to the East Ridge by December. It had been divided into four sections for the move.On December 17, 1985, military and civilian crews began the final operation. The Nevada Army National Guard, Montana National Guard, U.S. Army Reserve personnel from Butte and civilian workers took part in moving the sections up the mountain. The Butte-Silver Bow Public Archives records that the completed statue weighed 51 tons and was placed on the mountain in December 1985 with assistance from the Montana National Guard, Army Reserve and civilian crews. The statue was completed in December 1985, six years after O'Bill began the project. Its size was far beyond the five- to nine-foot monument originally discussed, and the finished figure ended up becoming one of the largest statues in the United States.A monument to mothersO'Bill had originally made the promise because of his wife's illness, but the completed monument was eventually dedicated to women and mothers more broadly. The official Our Lady of the Rockies organization describes the statue as nondenominational and says it is intended as a tribute to women and mothers. A memorial wall at the site carries the names of mothers from different parts of the world.The University of Montana describes Our Lady of the Rockies as a major Butte landmark. Its account says the 90-foot statue was completed in December 1985 after being conceived by O'Bill as a tribute to the Virgin Mary following his wife's recovery from cancer. The statue now sits on private land high above the city, and can be seen from much of Butte and from surrounding roads. O'Bill died in 2016, but Joyce survived him. The original reason for the statue therefore remains part of its history, while the monument itself has taken on a wider role in Butte. The project began with a personal promise in 1979, and by December 1985, a 90-foot statue stood on the East Ridge. Its construction involved volunteers, engineers, military crews and residents who spent years raising money and preparing the site. Our Lady of the Rockies remains above Butte today, standing on the Continental Divide with the city below.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Fresh flood threat for Nepal as barrier lake breaches near China border
articles.summary: South Asia News: A large barrier lake near the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers in Nepal has reportedly breached, raising fears of another su.
articles.body: A large barrier lake near the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers in Nepal has reportedly breached, raising fears of another surge of water into the Bhotekoshi River.Rasuwa chief district officer Narendra Pariyar said on Friday that the Nepali Army had informed him that the lake had breached, as cited by the Kathmandu Post.The development comes a day after Chinese authorities warned that the flood-formed lake was overflowing and faced a high risk of breaching as rising water levels continued to feed into it.China’s ministry of water resources said the lake had accumulated around 2 million cubic metres of water by Thursday morning and was already overflowing, heightening concerns over a possible breach.Chinese authorities said they were closely monitoring the lake, conducting flood simulations and hydrological assessments to determine the potential impact of a breach and prepare for emergency rescue and flood-control measures.The Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo originate in Tibet and merge before flowing into Nepal, where the river is known as the Bhotekoshi. It is the principal upper tributary of the Trishuli River.A glacier collapse in Tibet triggered severe flash floods and mudslides along the China-Nepal border, leaving at least 475 people dead and several missing, according to authorities in the two countries. The figures vary across agencies, reflecting differences in data collection, verification and coordination.Nepal is preparing to conduct an aerial reconnaissance mission over the Bhotekoshi River and surrounding areas of Rasuwa to assess the potential impact of the reported lake breach.An official at the Rescue Coordination Centre at Tribhuvan International Airport said helicopters stationed in Dhunche and other parts of Rasuwa would be deployed for the operation, with no additional aircraft being sent from Kathmandu.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Indian-origin US couple on group pilgrimage to Mount Kailash goes missing after Nepal-Tibet floods
articles.summary: US News: An Indian-origin US couple from Texas has gone missing during a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash after devastating flash floods and mudslides struck the Ne.
articles.body: An Indian-origin US couple from Texas has gone missing during a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash after devastating flash floods and mudslides struck the Nepal-Tibet border, with around 90 US citizens unaccounted for, according to US officials.Deepak Ahuja, 60, and his wife Madhu Ahuja, 57, had travelled from Texas on a group pilgrimage to Mount Kailash. Their daughters, Shreya and Ashna Ahuja, told the BBC that they lost contact with their parents shortly before the floods struck and have since approached US authorities and embassies in India, Nepal and China for information about their whereabouts.The US State Department said about 90 US citizens may have been impacted by the disaster, while three Americans have been rescued. Officials said the US embassy in Nepal was working with local authorities and tour operators to assist affected Americans.The disaster also affected at least 77 people travelling with the Isha Foundation on a Kailash pilgrimage. The group was at an immigration facility near the border when the flash flood hit, according to the BBC.Initial reports suggested an earthquake may have triggered an ice avalanche and landslide. However, the US Geological Survey later said its analysis indicated that the seismic energy was generated by a landslide itself. Rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering the landslide and flash flooding. Scientists said it was too early to determine whether climate change contributed to the specific disaster.Americans missing after Nepal floodsThe Associated Press reported that about 90 Americans remained unaccounted for a day after catastrophic flash floods engulfed the Nepal-Tibet border region. The State Department said it was not aware of any US deaths and confirmed that three Americans had been rescued.Many of the missing were travelling on pilgrimages to Mount Kailash, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.Among the missing are other Indian-origin US citizens, including 45-year-old Venus Rajnikant Patel and 72-year-old Long Island resident Jitendra Patel, AP reported.Nepal police said more than 500 tourists from 28 countries were missing, while Chinese state media reported hundreds missing in Tibet.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Banbury café owner seeks ideas for second pigeon mural update
articles.summary: Two years after a cafe's pigeon mural was controversially replaced, its owner plans a new design.
articles.body:
A cafe owner is calling on the local community to help him update its famous pigeon mural.

For more than three decades colourful artwork has featured on the side of the former Bridge Bar on Bridge Street in Banbury, Oxfordshire.

For many of those years, a huge image of a pigeon with its wings spread wide loomed over the street.

In 2024, owner of the now Power Cup café Tomas Kolbus decided the old work needed updating, so brought in artists to transform it, controversially painting over the bird.

He has now decided to involve the community in redesigning the work to better reflect the town and possibly to feature a new pigeon.

Kolbus said in 2024 the pigeon was in a bad way, so he approached the artists behind the original 30-year-old artwork to replace it.

He said the reaction was mixed, with not everyone happy at the change, but that people came around to the new design.

Two years on, and he said he was now working with artists from Banbury, Swindon and London on a new update, but wanted to make sure it reflected life in Banbury.

He said: "This year I decided, what shall we create? Another chapter on that wall.

"Not to delete everything, not to repaint it, just to add something more."

The mural is in a prominent location in Banbury, close to the bus and railway stations.

Kolbus said he was gathering information from people in the community, and wanted to create something that would remind people to slow down, relax and not to focus on stress.

As for the final design, he said it would remain a secret for now, but would probably feature a pigeon that was "funnier and more interesting".

articles.title: Epstein links and rape conviction cast shadow over Norway’s new royal family
articles.summary: As King Haakon of Norway ascends the throne after the death of his father, the former naval officer must steer a royal family in crisis towards calmer shores...
articles.body:
As King Haakon of Norway ascends the throne after the death of his father, the former naval officer must steer a royal family in crisis towards calmer shores.

The King, 53, has endured a string of royal scandals in recent years linked to his stepson, Marius Borg Høiby ; his wife Mette-Marit, now the Queen; and his sister, Martha-Louise.

Opinion polls suggest there is a crisis of confidence in the royal family. A survey found that one in three Norwegians wanted the monarchy to be abolished upon the death of King Harald .

The most damaging revelations have centred on Borg Høiby, 29, the new King's stepson, who was convicted of rape and assault in June and sentenced to four years in prison.

A few months before the trial began, the royal family was engulfed by another scandal as Norwegian media revealed that Mette-Marit had been a friend of Jeffrey Epstein in the early 2010s.

Less troublesome, but still a major part of Norway's public debate on their royal family, was Princess Martha-Louise's decision to marry a self-styled US shaman in August 2024.

King Haakon is arguably the outlier among his immediate family: placid, understated and determined to uphold their good name, come what may.

Born in 1973, he attended state schools in Norway as his parents were eager to ensure he grew up among "ordinary" Norwegians.

Having finished secondary school, he entered the Norwegian navy where he served as an officer on a torpedo boat.

He is a fan of skiing, surfing and music – which is how he met Mette-Marit at a 1999 music festival in Kristiansand.

Mette-Marit Tjessem Høiby was, at that time, a commoner and single mother to Marius, the child she had in a previous relationship with Morten Borg.

An entrepreneur and well-known figure on the Oslo party scene, Borg had convictions for assault and cocaine possession.

The then crown prince married Mette-Marit, who has said her "teenage rebellion was stronger than most people's", in 2001.

In 2004, Mette-Marit gave birth to a future queen, Ingrid Alexandra.

The King adopted Borg Høiby, then a boy, as his own son, and for a period the family enjoyed positive publicity, with Norwegians embracing them as a modern royal family.

In 2018, Mette-Marit was diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, a condition that required her to receive a lung transplant days before her son's rape conviction earlier this year.

Borg Høiby was a constant feature of Norwegian glossy magazines and tabloid headlines for years.

He was arrested for sexual offences in August 2024 and his trial gripped the nation, causing serious damage to the royal reputation.

In addition to the rape and assault convictions, he was convicted of filming a woman's genitals without her consent and breaking a restraining order. One of his victims was in court and wept as the verdict was read out.

The seven-week trial disclosed in detail the stepson's drug addiction, with self-made videos of sexual encounters and more than 800 electronic messages entered into evidence.

At the same time, the royal family was in the centre of a media storm over revelations that Mette-Marit had had a close relationship with Epstein, the US financier and convicted paedophile.

Emails obtained by Norwegian media showed that she had continued their relationship after he had been convicted of soliciting a minor. She later said she was " manipulated and deceived ".

In a 2011 email to Epstein disclosed by Norwegian media, Mette-Marit appeared to joke that she had googled him after his conviction for soliciting a minor, which she said "didn't look too good," before adding a smiley emoji.

In a 2012 email exchange, where Epstein said he was on a "wife hunt" in Paris, Mette-Marit joked in a reply that "Scandis [are] better wife material".

In another 2012 email, Mette-Marit asked Epstein for parenting advice about her son Borg Høiby.

"Is it inappropriate for a mother to suggest two naked women carrying a surfboard for my I5-year-old son's wallpaper?" she asked.

"Let them decide... stay out of it," Epstein replied.

In 2013, Mette-Marit stayed at Epstein's Florida house in Palm Beach for four days.

She has said she deeply regretted her friendship and has never been accused of any criminal wrongdoing linked to Epstein.

"[I] must take responsibility for not having investigated Epstein's background more thoroughly, and for not realising sooner what kind of person he was," she said.

Now, all eyes fall upon her husband, the new King, to see whether he can turn the page on so many years of scandal.

articles.title: UK soldiers could get paragliders to drop behind enemy lines
articles.summary: The Ministry of Defence is set to trial a UK-made system to allow troops to mount covert operations without aircraft.
articles.body:
British soldiers could soon be given powered paragliders to enable them to fly up to 200 miles behind enemy lines.

The backpack-sized gliders mean Royal Marine and Parachute Regiment troops could fly into hostile areas during the night without the need to drop from aircraft.

Manufacturer Blakcro, which is based in Wiltshire, say the machines can be assembled in eight minutes and launched on foot.

The Ministry of Defence is spending £6m on the system, with trials set to begin "in the coming months".

Defence Minister Luke Pollard said the government was building a "more resilient, homegrown defence supply chain and ensuring our armed forces receive the pioneering equipment that can give them the edge on the battlefield".

The paragliders, which have a range of up to 200 miles, can carry body armour, night vision equipment and weapon mounts.

The manufacturers say the titanium-framed machines can be used to enter hostile territory covertly as they are more difficult to detect by radar or sound than traditional aircraft.

The gliders will be powered by a fan but pilots will be expected to launch them on foot.

The technology is currently being used by other Nato member countries.

Blakcro, which employs 11 people, was founded in 2023 and has received government support for two other projects.

The company also works with the US Department of Defense.

The government has said it wants to spend more on UK-made defence equipment and bring smaller companies into the supply chain.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to increase defence spending after he resigned from Sir Keir Starmer's government in protest at its investment plans.

As defence secretary, he accused Starmer's government of having no clear timetable to reach the target of spending 3% of the UK's national income on defence.

He is expected to increase spending further - but will not be setting out any plans in his first Budget in October.

Instead, a revised defence plan will be set out as part of a wider government spending review in the spring.

A government spokesperson said: "The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe.

"The prime minister and chancellor are committed to fully funding the defence investment plan.

"At the spending review we will set out a pathway to meet our NATO commitment of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and will set a target date to hit 3% on that path."

articles.title: Japan killed more than 14,000 bears between April 2025 and January 2026 after record attacks on people; despite the cull, 6 people have been killed this year and the government plans to remove another 8,800 bears
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Japan killed more than 14,000 bears between April 2025 and January 2026 after record attacks on people; despite the cull, 6 people have been killed th.
articles.body: Japan killed more than 14,000 bears between April 2025 and January 2026 after record attacks on people; despite the cull, 6 people have been killed this year and the government plans to remove another 8,800 bearsAs Tokyo heats up, every year thousands in Japan head to Karuizawa in the Nagano prefecture. Located at the foot of Mount Asama, its bamboo-lined pathways and canopied forests make for the perfect tranquil escape. But along with humans even bears move to the area in search of food including mulberries, ants, leaves and cherry blossoms. Unlike most years, this time it has become a war, according to a report by The Guardian.Since the 1990s, Picchio, a small Japanese conservation and education group has been working to improve the coexistence between people and bears in the region. Staff respond to reported bear sightings with one of their three Karelians – a dog breed trained in the western US to chase away bears. When dogs aren’t enough, the Picchio team tranquilises and relocates bears deep in the forest.But as bear-human conflict increases in the country, not many are following this cue. Last year, bears attacked more than 230 people in the country, with 13 people killed, making it the deadliest year on record. Most attacks were in the mountainous northern prefectures of Akita and Iwate, where record-breaking heat affected the growth of beech nuts and acorns that bears rely on to fatten up for hibernation.Foreign governments – including the UK – issued travel advice warning of heightened bear risk. Insurance companies began offering specialised “bear insurance” to cover repairs to ransacked properties. Farmers installed animatronic wolves with glowing red eyes to frighten off the animals. Warning posters adorned lamp-posts.In Karuizawa, Hiroo Tamatani, the leader of Picchio’s bear team, says it has already captured 19 bears this year and responded to more than 130 sightings and incidents – up about 20% since this time last year. But there has been no rise in the actual number of bear damage incidents.According to the national government, a rise in bear attacks can be credited to the lack of skilled hunters in helping manage the population. Local associations have struggled to attract new members, with the number of licensed hunters falling by more than half since 1975. Left with few options, last year, the government relaxed the rules for shooting bears in populated areas, as officials laid traps across the country.As a result, from April 2025 through January 2026, Japan culled more than 14,000 bears, government data shows. That included about 12,000 Asiatic black bears (Ursus thibetanus)and 2,000 brown bears (Ursus arctos).Too many deaths?The high death toll has raised concerns among conservationists. Asiatic black bears are deemed vulnerable to extinction by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN), with fewer than 60,000 remaining worldwide. “If this level of trapping continues, we believe regional extinctions are a real possibility. We feel a profound sense of crisis,” said Yuko Muroya, chair of the Japan Bear and Forest Society (Kumamori), which focuses on conservation and coexistence.Japan is one of the Asiatic black bear’s last strongholds, with an estimated 42,000 bears. Still, removing what could amount to a quarter of the country’s population has seemingly done little to end conflict. Since April, six people have been killed and more than 35 attacked across at least nine prefectures – including some close to Tokyo – according to government statistics. In June, one Japanese city suspended nearly 100 schools after a bear was spotted in the area for the first time.Muroya added it is clear Japan’s heavy-handed approach to stopping the assaults is not working. Yet the government has announced a target of culling another 8,800 bears this fiscal year. “A government strategy focused solely on reducing bear numbers will not solve the bear problem until bears themselves are driven to extinction,” she says.“It’s a big reaction,” said biologist Dave Garshelis, co-chair of the IUCN’s bear specialist group and its Asiatic black bear expert team. “I think the [Japanese] government felt compelled to just get rid of these bears … This happened all of a sudden and they had no other alternative.”Until last year, Japan had adopted a more conservative approach. From 2008 to 2018, the country culled between 1,000 and 4,500 bears every year, alongside legal sport hunting of about 500 a year. That number, however, had been ticking up, with more than 9,000 bears killed in 2023-24 – another bad food year for the animals that led to six human fatalities.Whether or not Japan’s bear cull ultimately poses a global conservation concern, “really depends on how many they have”, said Garshelis.Shinsuike Koike, an ecologist at Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology, leads the Japan Bear Network, a nonprofit promoting coexistence through research. He is sceptical not just of the national figures, but also of global estimates. “In many countries, even the distribution of Asiatic black bears is not well understood,” he says. “I think it is impossible to estimate the global population with high accuracy.”In 2023, Koike says that in one study area of central Japan they found the Asiatic black bear population was growing at a rate of between 11% and 12% a year. He adds that under the right environmental conditions, it is possible that population growth in some parts of western Japan may reach 15%.That would mean, without hunting or culls, the country’s bear population would double every five years. Under such a scenario, killing 15% of bears every year would keep the population stable. Anything greater would trigger a decline.Globally, the IUCN says the Asiatic black bear population is shrinking. A 2024 study in the journal Scientific Reports found that the Asiatic black bear’s worldwide range has contracted by roughly half compared with records of distribution from the 19th and 20th centuries.A macabre outcomeThe tragedy that has unfolded in Japan over the past 16 months is essentially a macabre outcome of a conservation success story. Since the 1970s, Asiatic black bears have recolonised much of their former range on Japan’s largest island of Honshu. As people have traded village life for cities, farmland has returned to woodland, connecting bear habitat across thousands of kilometres.Of the 18 countries where Asiatic black bears are still found, “Japan has done the best job of them all as far as conserving this species,” Garshelis says. “The issue is they didn’t plan ahead for conservation success.”But Japan’s booming bear population has now run up against a sharp drop in forest foods. Kumamori’s researchers are documenting how the climate crisis is altering Japan’s forests. They have witnessed widespread dieback of Mongolian oak, acorns destroyed by grey weevils, poor seed production in Japanese beech and sharp declines in pollinating insects that have led to sparse berry yields.Critics say the spate of attacks in 2023 should have been a wake-up call for the government to adopt more proactive measures to prevent bear conflicts, rather than rely on hunting to severely slash numbers. “Despite the severe degradation of natural forests caused by climate change, bear specialists and the government simply watch the bears that come down from the mountains,” Muroya said.Kumamori plants nut-bearing trees, hoping to encourage the bears to stay in the woods. “In the past, Japan successfully maintained a separation between people and bears. We should learn how our ancestors achieved that coexistence. We should also learn from other countries, many of which have moved beyond policies focused solely on culling,” Muroya added.In November 2025, Japan’s environment ministry released its plan to protect against bear damage, with individual prefectures expected to implement the policies. It includes chasing bears away, installing fences to prevent bears from entering communities, removing fruit trees around homes, and conducting training response exercises for authorities. The ministry has also hired bear management officers for regional offices in eastern Japan, a government spokesperson told the Guardian.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Locals cautioned, driver reversed’: How a warning saved 26 Andhra pilgrims from Nepal floods
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A brief tea break and a warning from locals helped a group of Andhra Pradesh pilgrims narrowly escape the devastating flash floods in Nepal.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A brief tea break and a warning from locals helped a group of Andhra Pradesh pilgrims narrowly escape the devastating flash floods in Nepal, with the bus driver reversing to safety just minutes before the floodwaters swept through the route ahead.The group of 26 pilgrims from Tirupati had travelled to Nepal for the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra and was on its way from Kathmandu towards the China border when the near-disaster unfolded on August 25.The pilgrims had spent the previous two days at a hotel in Kathmandu due to a delay in visa clearances.They left the Nepalese capital at around 6am on August 25 and stopped along the route for a tea break.According to a pilgrim who later returned to Delhi, that brief halt proved crucial."In the last two days, we had to stay in a hotel in Kathmandu because we were late. On the morning of the 25th, we left Kathmandu for the China border at 6 AM. On the way, we stopped for a tea break."The pilgrim said another bus that had left with them was caught in the disaster and hit a bridge."Because of that stop, the bus that left with us hit a bridge. If we had stopped for a tea break, we would have also hit the bridge. We are 100 metres ahead of the floods."The danger became clearer when the driver of a bus travelling ahead alerted their driver about the approaching floodwaters and told him to move the vehicle immediately."The bus driver in front of us and some locals alerted the driver that the floods were coming and asked him to immediately move the bus. The bus driver immediately took us to a place where we were safe."The group then moved to safer ground and escaped the flash flood that devastated parts of the Nepal-China border region.The pilgrim expressed gratitude to those who helped them and to the governments that coordinated assistance during the crisis."We thank God and all of you. And also, the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, Mr. Chandra Babu and Mr. Nara Lokesh Babu, who always stood by us. We also thank the Government of Andhra Pradesh and the Government of India. By the grace of God, all of you and our families are reaching home safely. Thank you."The incident came as the Nepal flash flood death toll rose to 547 on Friday, with 977 people still missing, including foreign tourists and security personnel.Around 1,545 people have been rescued, while search operations continued across the affected districts.Authorities also warned of fresh flooding in the Bhotekoshi River area after a barrier lake formed near the Nepal-China border, with China issuing a Level-IV alert.Here are more Raksha Bandhan wishes, Bhadra kaal and Shubh Muhurat from The Times of India.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: A Texas farmer’s family has worked 6,000 acres for over a century; after his landlord sold 600 rented acres for a Google data center, he was given 60 days to leave
articles.summary: US News: Standing near the Haskell County border in West Texas, fourth-generation farmer Cheyenne Buerger can see industrial cranes building a huge Google faci.
articles.body: Standing near the Haskell County border in West Texas, fourth-generation farmer Cheyenne Buerger can see industrial cranes building a huge Google facility just over four miles to the northeast. Until recently, part of that same horizon was farmland he worked himself. After farming thousands of acres with his family for more than a century, Buerger was forced to give up 600 acres of rented farmland when his landlord suddenly sold the property to a developer clearing the site for the tech giant. The eviction gave the local farmer very little time to harvest his remaining crops and leave the land. "When I explained I had a crop on it, they said 'You can finish it, but that's it,'" Buerger said. "'You've got to be done in 60 days, and you're out." Losing the land near Haskell has taken away a large part of Buerger's local farming operation. Along with his family's 6,000 acres, where they grow cotton, wheat and milo, the rented fields gave the family more flexibility for crop rotations and livestock management. "It makes me feel a little threatened just from losing land to data centers," Buerger said. "We can't compete with that."Corporate expansion across rural TexasThe loss of farmland to technology projects is becoming more common across Texas, according to an investigation by The Texas Tribune. As major technology companies expand artificial intelligence and cloud computing, developers are moving into rural counties looking for large, flat and relatively cheap areas of land. Data from the Pew Research Center shows that about 67 per cent of data centres in the United States are located in rural areas. In Texas, low taxes and large amounts of available land have long attracted major industries, but the current growth of data centres has reached new levels. An analysis by The Texas Tribune found 335 operating data centres across Texas, with at least 248 more either planned or under construction. The fast conversion of farmland into large server campuses is causing concern among farmers who are increasingly competing with wealthy technology companies for land and other important resources, including groundwater and electricity.Growing pressure on farmlandThe expansion comes at a difficult time for Texas agriculture. The industry produces more than $963 billion in total economic activity and generates nearly $15 billion in annual exports, according to state production figures cited in the report. State officials have also criticised the choice of farmland for some of these projects. Speaking at a public forum on rural industrial development organised by The Texas Tribune in Granbury, Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller warned that turning fertile soil into technology sites could permanently reduce the state's ability to produce food. "They're building them on our most valuable, most fertile farmland," said Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller. "Once our farmland is gone and paved over, we'll never farm it again." The amount of land needed for some of these projects is enormous. Three major developments, Project Matador in the Panhandle, Project Pacifico in Pecos County and Project Meta in El Paso, are expected to cover at least 16,000 acres combined. That is roughly equal to 12,000 American football fields.Huge projects, huge energy needsIn Hereford, about 50 miles southwest of Amarillo, Google outlined plans for its multi-phase Project Roman during a public community meeting. Local farmer Darren Grotegut attended the meeting and learned that the first phase alone would use 3,700 acres for computing facilities. More land would be needed for solar and wind projects to provide electricity. Grotegut estimated that all four phases could eventually cover more than 180,000 acres. To reduce the large amount of water needed to cool the computer equipment, project representatives said some nearby farmland could be converted into native grasslands to help protect local aquifers. The pressure on rural land is not limited to data centres. Clean energy monitoring company Cleanview says 240 utility-scale solar farms are now operating on rural Texas land. By 2024, about 1.5 million acres of former farmland across the state had been converted to solar energy production. For farmers such as Buerger, the future of tenant farming in West Texas looks increasingly uncertain. He still hauls cotton seed across his remaining pastures to feed cattle while construction crews put up steel frames on the fields he once rented. As investors and energy developers continue buying large connected areas of land across Jones and Haskell counties, family farmers have fewer options for finding replacement acreage. Rising land prices linked to industrial development are also making it harder for them to compete. Across the region, farming communities are facing lasting changes in how land, water and electricity are used.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: US News: A New Hampshire man allegedly stole a rescue truck from firefighters battling a blaze at his own home, drove over active fire hoses and crashed into a.
articles.body: A New Hampshire man allegedly stole a rescue truck from firefighters battling a blaze at his own home, drove over active fire hoses and crashed into a fire engine before fleeing the scene, authorities said.According to the New York Post, 30-year-old Nestor Roman II of Dalton faces multiple felony and misdemeanor charges over the early-morning incident on August 25. The fire broke out near Faraway Road and Mountain Road, with several nearby departments responding to assist Dalton Fire & Rescue.New Hampshire State Police said troopers were heading to the scene around 3:50 am when they learned that a Whitefield Fire & Rescue vehicle had been stolen.Roman allegedly got behind the wheel of an F550 rescue truck shortly before 5 am while firefighters were still fighting the blaze.Officials said Roman drove around a Whitefield fire engine, nearly hitting two firefighters and narrowly missing a third who could have been trapped between the vehicles. He then allegedly crashed the stolen truck into the fire engine and a pickup.The rescue truck also ran over multiple water-supply lines, including two charged hoses being used to battle the fire. The hoses were not damaged, officials said.Roman allegedly continued driving, striking a firefighter's personal vehicle and damaging wooden fences at two nearby properties before fleeing.The chase ended several miles away after a Dalton homeowner reported that the stolen rescue vehicle had crashed on their property. The homeowner also told police that the driver was allegedly trying to take items from the porch.Troopers found Roman there and took him into custody after he was initially uncooperative, police said.Roman faces three felony counts of reckless conduct with a deadly weapon, burglary and two counts of theft by unauthorized taking. He also faces several misdemeanor charges, including conduct after an accident, obstructing government administration, resisting arrest, driving after suspension and driving over a fire hose without consent.Despite significant damage, the Whitefield fire engine remained operational and firefighters eventually extinguished the blaze.Officials said the house was a "complete loss."The New Hampshire State Fire Marshal's Office is investigating the cause of the fire. No firefighters were physically injured in the incident, Dalton Fire & Rescue said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Time limit, School Mode and more: 11 changes that Meta promises it will add for teens on Instagram and Facebook
articles.summary: Tech News News: Facebook parent company Meta settled cases involving youth mental health and data privacy claims with 52 bipartisan attorneys general across US states.
articles.body: Facebook parent company Meta settled cases involving youth mental health and data privacy claims with 52 bipartisan attorneys general across US states, territories and Washington, D.C. for approximately $18 billion. The Mark Zuckerberg-led company has committed to rolling out major protective overhauls for under-18 users across Instagram and Facebook. The settlement concluded a federal trial in Oakland, California, which scrutinised how social media platforms impact adolescent well-being.While Meta agreed to the financial distribution terms and sweeping platform adjustments, the company maintained that it committed no wrongdoing. Under the formal agreement, the financial settlement will be paid out to participating jurisdictions over a 10-year timeline to support youth online safety programs and other state initiatives.11 core protections Meta promises for teens and parentsIn a blog, Meta has committed to implementing comprehensive behavioural, algorithmic and privacy modifications designed to foster healthier screen habits and give parents greater oversight:Combined two-hour daily time cap: A default daily limit of two hours will apply across both Facebook and Instagram combined, counting total scrolling time across duplicate or multiple profiles. Minors can only disable the limit with verified parental permission.Automatic ‘Night Mode’: Between midnight and 6:00 am, access to Feeds, Stories, Reels and Explore pages will be automatically blocked for minors.‘School Mode’ notifications: Standard push notifications will be muted by default from 8:00 am to 3:00 pm, though critical account security notices and direct messages will still go through.Regular screen-time checks: Automated screen-time alerts will trigger after 15 minutes of uninterrupted browsing, followed by additional usage prompts when total daily screen time reaches 60 and 90 minutes.Non-algorithmic feed choices: Young users will have the option to set an non-personalised, non-algorithmic feed as their default view, with regular reminders about the feature, while parents can enforce the setting.Manual autoplay controls: Teens and parents can turn off video autoplay, requiring an intentional swipe or tap before another video begins playing.Hidden Like and Reaction counts: The visibility of reaction and like tallies on their own posts and those of other users will be hidden by default for minor accounts.Prohibiting extreme cosmetic filters: Adding to existing bans on cosmetic surgery filters, Meta will prohibit youth accounts from accessing extreme cosmetic and makeup enhancement filters.Enhanced age assurance systems: The company said that it is deploying upgraded AI models to identify and take down accounts belonging to children under 13, while placing users aged 13 to 17 in protective experiences even if they enter adult birthdays.According to the company, it will continue advocating for federal legislation requiring mobile app stores to verify user ages and require parental consent prior to downloads.13+ content guardrails: Teen profiles will automatically default to 13+ age-appropriate content settings based on movie rating criteria and parent feedback to ensure minors don’t see or follow inappropriate accounts.Restricting stranger contact: Finally, Instagram and Facebook will make minor profiles default to private mode, block contact from suspicious adult accounts and make it tougher for unfamiliar adults to find teen profiles.Meta said the direct messaging features will still be available outside of Nite Mode and School Mode and the two-hour time limit so that teens can still connect with family and friends.Get articles.title: Sudan conflict: Two-year curfew lifted in Khartoum
articles.summary: The military authorities retook control of the city 18 months ago, but the conflict continues elsewhere.
articles.body:
Sudan's military-led government has lifted a curfew and state of emergency in Khartoum imposed more than two years ago, state media says.

The authorities are taking this step 18 months after the army seized back control of the capital from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which it has been fighting in a civil war now in its fourth year.

But clashes continue in the south and west, with mounting evidence that the war is spilling across Sudan's borders.

More than two million of the roughly five million people who fled Khartoum after war erupted in April 2023 have returned to the city since fighting there ended in March 2025, according to the International Organization for Migration.

The aim of lifting the curfew is to help restore normal life to the capital.

The government has reopened the city's main airport for some flights and is encouraging businesses and embassies to come back.

But residents still struggle to rebuild their livelihoods.

Many have found widespread damage with many buildings looted. And they have to cope with constant power blackouts, due to alleged RSF drone attacks on electricity infrastructure and a lack of government funds to carry out repairs.

"The targeting of the electricity sector in particular was very significant," a spokesperson for the Khartoum state government, Altayeb Saadeldin, told the Reuters news agency, listing looting of copper wires and fuel and other components, as well as drone attacks, as reasons for the outages.

An RSF source responded that the allegations were "incorrect and army propaganda".

Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity

Despite lifting the state of emergency, the authorities remain wary of RSF infiltration. The Sudan News Agency said security patrols would continue operating across the state and locals traveling at night would need to carry identification documents.

Reports compiled by BBC Monitoring say the army continues to carry out security sweeps across greater Khartoum, targeting alleged RSF sleeper cells, undocumented foreigners and criminals involved in illegal activities.

In the meantime, there is growing concern that the war is drawing in neighbouring countries.

Chad is accusing the Sudanese army of carrying out an air strike that hit a military convoy in Ennedi-Est province, about 100km (62 miles) inside Chadian territory, on 20 August. It has reportedly put its forces along the border on maximum alert.

Sudan has rejected the charge, saying it is surprised that its army was blamed without an independent investigation.

In a statement, the foreign ministry said it "affirms that the Sudanese army fulfils its constitutional duty to defend Sudan's sovereignty, security and territorial integrity, and to confront the threats facing the country, while remaining committed to respecting the sovereignty of neighbouring states and refraining from targeting their territories".

Sudan accuses Chad of permitting the passage of RSF military supplies delivered by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) through its airports and border crossings.

The UAE and Chad deny the allegations despite similar findings by UN experts and investigative reports by international media.

The attack on the Chadian convoy prompted the US Senior Adviser for Arab and African Affairs, Massad Boulos to express "deep concern" about the risk of Sudan's war threatening regional peace and stability.

Boulos has been urging the parties to immediately accept a humanitarian truce. He has grown increasingly frustrated with the Sudanese military, which refuses to engage in a peace process unless the RSF disarms and withdraws from the territory it has occupied.

"The United States condemns the SAF's recent air strikes inside Chad," Boulos wrote in a post on X. "There is no military solution to this conflict - and absolutely no justification for expanding the violence beyond Sudan's borders.

"External financial and military support to the warring parties must stop," he added.

This month the US envoy presented a draft resolution to the UN Security Council that would extend a 2005 weapons embargo on Darfur - the stronghold of the RSF - across the entire country and include a ban on attack drones, which are increasingly used by both sides.

Sudan's government and army have rejected the proposal. According to local media reports officials argue that this unfairly equates the recognised national military with a paramilitary force and restricts its ability to defend citizens against an insurgency.

articles.title: Whitby holiday-let plans near historic viaduct refused
articles.summary: Deer habitat is among the concerns raised over the proposed Whitby development.
articles.body:
Plans to build four holiday-let units near a Victorian viaduct have been refused following opposition from residents and concerns about the impact on the landscape and wildlife.

Developer Knapton & Knapton had applied to build the accommodation on Riverside Walk, off Larpool Lane, close to the Grade II listed Larpool Viaduct near Whitby.

More than 30 objections were submitted to North Yorkshire Council, raising concerns over ecology, heritage, highway impacts and the design of the proposed development.

One resident said the site was a refuge for local wildlife and warned construction work could damage a "thriving environment".

The units would have been built on land close to existing visitor accommodation, with the scheme also including new parking areas, landscaping and improvements to the access road.

In planning documents, the applicants said the development would provide "market-leading, high-end modular accommodation" that would be sensitive to the surrounding landscape and "enhance the experience of visitors and the wider public".

However, council planning officers concluded the proposal would cause "significant visual harm" to the setting of the viaduct, which was completed in 1884.

A report said that while additional tourist accommodation could bring some economic benefits, those benefits would be limited and did not outweigh the harm identified to the heritage asset.

North Yorkshire Council's conservation officer also warned that increasing development around the viaduct had reduced its historic setting in recent decades.

The officer said any further development would risk eroding the site's remaining "green setting" and would cause "clear harm" to the significance of the structure.

The Local Democracy Reporting Service said ecology concerns were also raised during the application process.

Objector Stephen Clough said the embankment was home to "families of deer" and provided a safe route for wildlife moving through the area.

"We feel that disruption, in the form of construction work, to this balanced ecosystem would be detrimental to the area and its ability to support such a thriving environment," he said.

The council's ecology officer said: "It could not be concluded that the scheme would avoid causing significant ecological harm."

The site lies south of Whitby town centre and north-east of Ruswarp, bordered by purpose-built holiday accommodation to the north and south.

The application was refused by North Yorkshire Council earlier this month.

articles.title: Nepal floods: Toll climbs past 550 on third day as rescuers race against time amid fresh threat
articles.summary: South Asia News: Three days after devastating flash floods tore through Nepal’s Himalayan river valleys, the death toll has risen to 579, according to the National Dis.
articles.body: Three days after devastating flash floods tore through Nepal’s Himalayan river valleys, the death toll has risen to 579, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, while thousands remain missing.Scientists are now working to reconstruct the sequence of events, but the precise trigger behind the glacial collapse that set off the floods remains unclear.The flooding struck areas around Timure and Syaphrubesi, near the Nepal-China border, destroying or damaging roads, bridges, buildings and other infrastructure before surging into the Trishuli river system.The floodwaters swept away people, vehicles and structures, leaving several settlements cut off from the rest of the region.On the third day, the scale of the disaster continues to emerge. Search and rescue teams are scouring riverbanks and downstream areas for survivors and missing people, while authorities are recovering bodies from locations far beyond the initial impact zone. The focus has also shifted to assessing the extent of the destruction and restoring access to affected communities.How many people have died?The death toll has risen to 579, but the figure is not considered final as search operations continue and authorities reconcile records from different districts. Hundreds of those caught in the disaster were foreigners who had travelled to the affected areas for work, guided treks or pilgrimages.The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 3,253 people had been rescued by helicopter, while more than 150 injured people were taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.With thousands still missing, identifying those killed has emerged as a major challenge. Police are photographing recovered bodies, collecting fingerprints, conducting post-mortems and taking DNA samples where required. In cases where facial identification is possible, photographs are being used to help families establish whether a missing relative has been found.DNA samples are being sent to Kathmandu for analysis at the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology and the Nepal Police Central Forensic Science Laboratory. Authorities are also preparing for the possibility that some victims may remain unidentified, as cited by the Kathmandu Post.Fear of more floodingAuthorities remained on high alert after a newly formed barrier lake near the Nepal-China border began overflowing, raising fears of another flash flood in a region already devastated by the disaster two days earlier. The earlier floods killed more than 500 people and left over 1,500 missing.Nepal’s disaster management authorities said satellite imagery and preliminary assessments indicated that an upstream river had been blocked, causing water to accumulate and form a growing lake. A breach could release a sudden surge downstream, posing a fresh threat to already affected communities and disrupting ongoing rescue operations.Satellite imagery released by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed that the lake had formed in the same area where a glacial detachment occurred on Wednesday, triggering the chain of events that caused widespread flooding and destruction downstream.CCTV reported that the lake’s barrier was located more than 10 km from Gyirong Port, a key border crossing with Nepal that was inundated by mud and floodwater. The lake is at an elevation of about 2,950 metres, nearly 1,000 metres above Gyirong Port, increasing concerns over the potential impact of a sudden breach.Rescue operations continueMore than 4,400 police personnel have been deployed for search and rescue operations, alongside teams from the Nepali Army and the Nepal Armed Police Force. According to Nepal Police, security forces have so far rescued or provided primary assistance to 1,473 people across Nuwakot, Rasuwa and Dhading.Rescue efforts have been complicated by extensive damage to roads and bridges, which has cut off several affected areas and restricted ground access.Authorities are therefore relying heavily on helicopters to reach isolated communities, evacuate people and support operations in locations that remain difficult to access.Nepal has declined offers from several countries, including India and China, to deploy specialised search-and-rescue teams as it responds to one of its worst flood disasters in years, saying its own security agencies have the capacity to manage the ongoing operations.However, Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal clarified that the government had not rejected assistance from friendly countries or the wider international community.He said Nepal remained open to seeking international technical expertise if rescue operations involved specialised challenges, particularly in tunnels or other complex structures.EAM Jaishankar receives 21 Tamil Nadu pilgrimsExternal affairs minister S Jaishankar on Friday received 21 Tamil Nadu pilgrims who were rescued from the devastating floods in Nepal and brought back to India.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said another 63 Indian nationals working at the Trishuli One hydropower project were rescued on Thursday. “In addition to these 21 Indian nationals, yesterday we gave you an update about 63 Indian nationals who are working at the Trishuli One hydropower project. They were also rescued yesterday,” he said.Jaiswal said authorities were currently unable to establish contact with 320 Indian nationals, who are being treated as missing or uncontactable. He also said around 400 Indian nationals stranded on the Chinese side of the Nepal-China border were safe, with the Indian Embassy in Beijing coordinating with local authorities to facilitate their evacuation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Norway mourns King Harald as Haakon VIII ascends throne
articles.summary: Mourners gather outside the palace as royals, politicians and citizens remember a beloved king, whose son has adopted the family motto "all for norway".
articles.body:
Norwegians, politicians and royals are grieving the death of beloved King Harald V, as a period of national mourning begins and his son King Haakon VIII assumes the throne.

After Harald's death was announced early on Friday, crowds amassed at the royal palace in Oslo, laying flowers and flags, some mourners visibly in tears.

Hours later, the new king met government ministers for an extraordinary council of state meeting, after which the 53-year-old announced he was taking on the royal family's motto "All for Norway".

Harald died peacefully in hospital at 06:35 local time (04:35 GMT) aged 89, after receiving treatment there for a rare blood condition since last week.

The late monarch has been described as an inclusive, transparent and empathetic "people's king" who modernised the Norwegian monarchy.

European royals, including King Charles III - whose mother Queen Elizabeth II was Harald's second cousin - as well as political leaders and ordinary citizens, paid tribute to his service and the stability he brought to the country.

Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".

In a televised memorial address - one of multiple eulogies by ministers - he said the late king's "legacy lives on" and offered condolences to the royal family and Queen Sonja, who would have celebrated her 58th wedding anniversary with Harald on Saturday.

Norwegian national footballer Erling Haaland thanked Harald for "everything you meant to Norway" in a post on Instagram, adding that it had been an honour to meet him earlier in the summer at the palace following the Fifa World Cup.

In the country's capital, Norwegians shared their grief and affection for the late king.

"I personally will say he was everything for us, especially being an immigrant," Biteya Terfassa, an Oslo resident who was born in Ethiopia, told news agency Reuters outside the palace.

"He made us feel at home and he made us feel loved. So he was like a grandfather that I never had."

At noon, the Norwegian Armed Forces honoured Harald with a funeral salute of 21 shots from Akershus Fortress in central Oslo.

Later on Friday, a procession left the chapel at Rikshospitalet, where Harald died, and headed to the palace.

Norway has declared a period of national mourning until the day of his funeral, which has not yet been announced. Flags will be flown at half-mast, while his portrait will be displayed, candles lit and moments of silence held at professional events.

All non work-related social events will be cancelled or postponed. Oslo Mayor Anne Lindboe, who was due to get married on Friday, even postponed her wedding .

King Haakon, who is Harald's younger child, is now the monarch and his wife Mette-Marit queen.

He is due to take an oath before the Norwegian parliament on Tuesday and will later participate in a consecration service - a stripped-down version of a corronation, which Norway no longer has.

His daughter, the 22-year-old Ingrid Alexandra, who joined her father to meet ministers at the palace on Friday, is next in line to the throne as crown princess after the rules of succession changed in 1990 to allow firstborn women to inherit the crown.

Haakon assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year.

Now-Queen Mette-Marit came under scrutiny earlier this year when it was revealed that she had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she has publicly apologised.

Later in the year, she received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care.

Meanwhile, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing.

Høiby is not a member of the royal family, but was raised with them since he was four years old, when now-King Haakon married his mother.

Although Harald remained popular until his death, a poll for newspaper Aftenposten earlier this year found that support for the monarchy had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.

However, Norwegian royal experts told the BBC that the new king, while facing questions about the turbulence surrounding his family, was respected, hard-working and, they believed, able to move forward despite the challenges.

articles.title: 'Terrorist connection' over Trump Turnberry vandalism charges
articles.summary: Seven people accused of causing damage at Trump's resort could receive longer sentences if convicted.
articles.body:
Seven people accused of vandalism at Donald Trump's Turnberry golf resort have been charged with an offence alleged to have a "terrorist connection".

The allegation is contained in an indictment lodged with the High Court of Justiciary in Glasgow over the incident that happened at the Ayrshire resort during a protest on 8 March 2025.

It states that the offence was aggravated under Section 31 of the Counter-Terrorism Act 2008, as amended by the Counter-Terrorism and Sentencing Act 2021, because it had a "terrorist connection".

The Defend Our Juries group has criticised the move, claiming the accused could face "far longer prison sentences" despite not being charged with terrorism offences.

Kieran Robson, 35, Uzma Bashir, 56, Ricky Southall, 34, Autumn Taylor Ward, 22, Rebecca Sian Davies, 29, John Moxley, 58, and Dylan Chiaramello, 24, were all charged with criminal damage following the protest.

It is alleged the group dug up turf and sprayed weedkiller on the course, caused flooding by damaging a sprinkler system, and damaged a light.

Prosecutors also allege that slogans including "Free Gaza", "Free Palestine" and "Gaza is not for sale" were daubed on the course and buildings, along with offensive messages directed at Trump.

The seven were due to appear at the High Court in Glasgow next Monday, but the Scottish Courts and Tribunals Service said on Friday that the hearing had been adjourned, with the next hearing due to take place in October.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

Robson also faces an allegation that he committed the offence while on bail. The indictment states that he had been granted bail at Edinburgh Sheriff Court on 9 January 2025.

The allegation comes after four members of Palestine Action received longer prison sentences in June after being convicted over a raid on a factory operated by Israeli defence company Elbit Systems.

More than £1m of damage was caused during that incident and the judge concluded there was a terrorist connection.

Human rights groups and supporters of those convicted criticised the sentences as disproportionate.

Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK in July 2025.

The Court of Appeal later upheld the government's decision, saying the group had "overtly promoted unlawful violence amounting to terrorism".

The group's co-founder Huda Ammori is seeking permission to challenge the implementation of the ban at the UK Supreme Court.

The US government designated Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation on Wednesday.

The Trump administration said the move was part of action against what it described as "far-left extremists".

articles.title: Israel reports killing of senior Hamas member in Jenin
articles.summary: The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it killed a senior Hamas member and two other militants in an airstrike in the city of Jenin in the West Bank. The Hamas...
articles.body:
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it killed a senior Hamas member and two other militants in an airstrike in the city of Jenin in the West Bank.

The Hamas member was involved in the financing and carrying out of attacks on Israeli civilians, the military and the Shin Bet domestic security service said on Friday evening.

He was also said to have been responsible for the Islamist terrorist organization's activities in the Jenin refugee camp.

Weapons were allegedly found in the car of those killed. The Israeli military did not initially provide any details regarding the identity of the Hamas member's two accomplices.

Last year, the Israeli army carried out a large-scale offensive against Palestinian militants in the city, as well as in two other refugee camps in the West Bank. Numerous people were killed, tens of thousands were driven from their homes, and massive destruction was caused.

According to the Israeli army, what it called the "Jenin terrorist network" was allegedly dismantled during this operation.

The situation in the occupied West Bank has deteriorated further since the Hamas massacre in Israel on October 7, 2023 and the resulting Gaza War.

According to the Palestinian health ministry, more than 1,100 Palestinians have since been killed in the West Bank during Israeli military operations, armed clashes and Palestinian attacks. Violence by radical Israeli settlers against Palestinians has also risen sharply.

articles.title: Nepal floods: Kathmandu agrees to foreign rescue help after pressure; India acts on its 'request'
articles.summary: India News: Nepal has agreed to accept foreign assistance for rescue operations after initially refusing the same as the scale of devastation from the floods cont.
articles.body: Nepal has agreed to accept foreign assistance for rescue operations after initially refusing the same as the scale of devastation from the floods continued to overwhelm relief efforts, The Kathmandu Post reported on Friday. India moved quickly to respond to Kathmandu's request for specialised support.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India was preparing to send a tunnel rescue team, with a reconnaissance team being flown in first to assess the situation and identify the equipment needed. India is also sending a medical team and has offered Bailey bridges along with technical teams to restore connectivity in affected areas."As requested by Nepal, we are preparing to send a tunnel rescue team, for which a recce team is being flown in first to assess the on-ground situation and what sort of equipment will be required. We are also sending a medical team to Nepal. In addition, we have also offered Bailey bridges along with associated technical teams so that connectivity can be restored quickly in the affected parts of Nepal and we can help in rescue and relief efforts... One Bailey bridge is already in Nepal and can be deployed for relief and connectivity efforts,” the MEA spokesperson Jaiswal said.Why Nepal agreedNepal reversed its earlier decision amid mounting pressure from countries whose nationals remain missing in the flood-hit areas. Several governments had urged Kathmandu to allow their specialist search-and-rescue teams to assist in locating survivors.“We received massive pressure from the international community to allow at least search-and-rescue teams and some experts because their citizens have also gone missing in the floods. We are allowing a limited number of experts in certain areas,” The Kathmandu Post reported quoting a senior government official.The decision also came as rescue operations made limited progress, with dozens of people still unaccounted for inside hydropower tunnels in Rasuwa and Nuwakot. The scale of the disaster has further increased the need for specialised tunnel-rescue expertise.Nepal also has limited capacity for DNA testing and forensic identification of bodies. Foreign experts will therefore assist with identifying the dead and ensuring that remains can be handed over to families as quickly as possible.India dispatches 3rd consignment of aidIndia also dispatched its third consignment of humanitarian assistance to Nepal. The 10-tonne shipment included portable generators, dignity kits, food packets and water purification tablets, while an 11-member team of doctors, paramedics and tunnel-rescue specialists travelled on the same flight.The latest consignment takes India's total relief assistance to Nepal to 57.5 tonnes since August 26. The earlier shipments included temporary shelters, blankets, hygiene kits, solar lamps, medicines, dewatering pumps, generators, kitchen sets and food supplies.India has also offered Bailey bridges to help restore connectivity, with Jaiswal noting that one such bridge is already in Nepal and can be deployed for relief operations.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Indian-origin New York teen and her mother among Americans missing in Nepal: Rashi wanted to do a solo Hindu pilgrimage
articles.summary: US News: 54-year-old Rekha Shashidharan and her daughter 14-year-old Rashi Shashidharan, both from New York, are on the list of 90 Americans missing in the dev.
articles.body: 54-year-old Rekha Shashidharan and her daughter 14-year-old Rashi Shashidharan, both from New York, are on the list of 90 Americans missing in the devasting landslide and flood in Nepal. Family members called every helpline number but there is no information about them yet. They are hopeful that the mother-daughter duo are probably somewhere safe.Shekhar Agarwal told CNN from Mumbai that his niece Rashi, an eighth grader, had originally planned to the Hindu pilgrimage solo and had been very excited. Rashi's mother, Shekhar's sister, Rekha eventually decided to accompanied her so that Rashi would not be travelig alone. Now both of them are missing.Agarwal said as far as he knew, the mother-daughter had spent a few days in Kathmandu to acclimate to the higher altitude of the Himalayas, before continuing north toward the Chinese border with the tour group. Agarwal last spoke to them on Wednesday 7.30 am (local time). They said they were planning to go the immigration checkpoint around noon that day before crossing into Tibet.Within an hour of their conversation, the glacier broke and brought the devastating flood devastating towns and villages on the riverbank.“After that, there was radio silence, nothing, no contact whatsoever,” Agrawal said. He thinks the mother and daughter may have still been in their hotel at the time.“Whatever (phone) numbers the internet or television or friends are giving us, we are trying to contact them,” Agrawal said. Many numbers provided for those seeking information about loved ones didn’t even work; and the ones that did work had no information to offer.Agarwal said the situation makes him feel helplessand he can't do much apart from hoping that his sister and niece are probably safe somewhere. “We are hoping for the best because these kinds of things have happened earlier also, and we have seen cases where people have walked after three days, four days, five days,” Agarwal said. “Right now, the only thing that you can do is be hopeful.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nepal flood devastation revealed in satellite imagery
articles.summary: Before-and-after images show villages, bridges and a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing washed away by devastating floodwaters.
articles.body:
New satellite imagery has revealed the scale of the devastation along Nepal's Trishuli River caused by Wednesday's deadly flash flood, triggered by a glacier collapse.

Before-and-after images show how sections of the valley, where a torrent of floodwater and debris surged through, destroyed villages, bridges and hydroelectric power stations.

More than 550 people have been killed, Nepalese officials say, with hundreds more missing.

Among the worst-hit locations reviewed by BBC Verify was a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing, which was engulfed by a rush of floodwater and captured on camera.

The satellite imagery from US-based intelligence firm Vantor, shows the site has been almost entirely washed away. Shocking CCTV footage showed the moment as the deluge of water swept over buildings as people tried to escape.

Damage and mud can be seen more than 2.5km (1.5 miles) upstream, reaching 100m (330 ft) above the area it first hit.

A few miles further south is the village of Timure, which has now largely disappeared.

The walls of the valley at this point are steep, reaching up to 50m above the water line. The image shows most of the houses perched on this slope are now gone or covered in mud.

A further 10km (eight miles) downstream, where the Trishuli River winds through Syapru Besi, satellite imagery now shows the village covered by mud, rock and other debris. Houses and other structures have disappeared, including bridges and a hydroelectric power station.

One of the larger villages to be struck by the full force of the flood was Trishuli, where some of the earliest verified footage of the disaster emerged from.

A satellite image of the town and surrounding agricultural land, which is about 45km (28 miles) downstream from the border, show an entire neighbourhood has been essentially washed away.

Verified videos of the town show a bridge collapsing as the river surges forward. At the very same moment from ground level, footage filmed from inside a bus shows people crying out in distress and trying to flee as they see the water rushing down the river.

Other dramatic videos show people sheltering inside a house, peering over the edge of a balcony as they watch a torrent of floodwater wash away almost everything around them, knocking large metal debris and a vehicle toward the building.

Somehow the house remains intact and survivors can be seen in a second verified video standing surrounded by mud once the floodwater had receded.

Imagery from satellite provider Planet Labs released today has also provided a clearer view of the disaster's origins at the collapsed glacier, the moment of which has been captured on a verified drone video.

The satellite image shows an enormous chunk of the glacier has fallen away, carving an enormous path of rock and debris where water rushed through the valley.

At the base of the landslide, trees and other vegetation have been stripped at a height of more than 300m above the riverbed.

This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.

Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts.

Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly.

But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake.

Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised.

The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area.

The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead.
