articles.title: 72-year-old South Korean man entered Japan on a 15-day visa, lived there for 33 years before being arrested
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A 72-year-old South Korean man who entered Japan on a 15-day visa in 1993 is now facing arrest after allegedly remaining in the country for about 33 y.
articles.body: A 72-year-old South Korean man who entered Japan on a 15-day visa in 1993 is now facing arrest after allegedly remaining in the country for about 33 years. The man, identified in Japanese reports as Mun Jong-gi, entered Japan in September 1993 using his younger brother's passport, according to police. He reportedly came to the country hoping to find better-paid work than he could get in South Korea and subsequently supported himself through day labour and casual jobs. His long stay eventually came to police attention after authorities received information about a suspected illegal resident in June 2026. He was arrested by Shizuoka Prefectural Police on August 26 on suspicion of violating Japan's immigration laws.South Korean man entered Japan in 1993 on a 15-day stayPolice say the man arrived in Japan in September 1993 and was granted permission to remain for only 15 days. Investigators allege that he entered using his younger brother's passport. Rather than returning to South Korea when his authorised stay ended, he remained in Japan and continued living and working there. His reported motivation was largely economic, with police saying he had hoped to earn more money in Japan than he could in his home country. Over the following decades, he is believed to have established a life in Japan without obtaining legal long-term residency status.His 33-year stay came to light after a police tipThe man's unusually long stay was not discovered through a routine check dating back to the beginning of his residence, according to the available reports. Instead, police received information in June 2026 concerning a suspected illegal resident. That information prompted an investigation by Shizuoka Prefectural Police, which eventually led officers to the man in Yaizu, Shizuoka Prefecture. Police arrested him on August 26, 2026, after investigating his immigration status. He reportedly admitted to the allegations during questioning. The circumstances of how he managed to remain in Japan for so many years without being detected are still being investigated, and available reports do not establish that authorities simply failed to notice him continuously for all 33 years.Why police refer to roughly 26 years of illegal residenceAlthough the man appears to have remained in Japan for about 33 years, the legal timeline is more complicated. Japan's rules regarding overstaying changed in February 2000, when illegal residence became subject to criminal punishment under the revised immigration law. Police therefore allege that the offence covered by the current arrest dates from February 2000 rather than from the end of his original 15-day permission in 1993. This means the man is believed to have lived in Japan continuously for around 33 years, while the period covered by the alleged criminal offence is roughly 26 years. The distinction is important because describing the case simply as a "33-year criminal overstay" would not accurately reflect the legal circumstances reported by Japanese authorities.Man reportedly survived through casual workDuring his years in Japan, the man is reported to have supported himself through day jobs and other casual employment. Police say he had originally travelled to Japan because he expected to find better-paid work there. Details about his employers and the precise nature of his work over the decades have not been fully disclosed in the available reports. It is also unclear how he managed other aspects of everyday life, including accommodation and official administrative procedures, during such a prolonged period without valid residence status. Those unanswered questions are part of what makes the case unusual, but they should not be filled with speculation.Japan had far more overstayers when he arrivedThe man's arrival coincided with a period when Japan had a much larger population of people who had remained after their authorised stays expired. Japanese Justice Ministry figures cited in reporting show that Japan had about 298,646 visa overstayers in 1993, the year he entered the country. By January 2026, the number had fallen to 68,488. The sharp decline reflects decades of changes in immigration enforcement and Japan's immigration system. His case therefore dates back to a very different period in Japan's immigration landscape, when the number of overstayers was several times higher than it is today.Police investigation is continuingThe man remains at the centre of an immigration investigation following his August 26 arrest. While he has reportedly admitted to the allegation, an arrest does not itself constitute a final court finding of guilt. Japanese authorities will determine the next steps under the country's immigration and criminal procedures. As of the latest available reporting, there had been no final court ruling or reported deportation decision.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Man died after 'severe turbulence' on Singapore Airlines flight
articles.summary: Lawyers for Linda Kitchen said her husband was "fatally injured" after the flight dropped 6,000 ft.
articles.body:
A widow whose husband died after "severe turbulence" on a flight has begun legal action against the airline.

Lawyers for Linda Kitchen, 74, from Thornbury near Bristol, who broke her back during the incident, said her husband, Geoff, 73, was "fatally injured" when the Singapore Airlines flight from London Heathrow suddenly dropped around 6,000 ft (1,828 metres).

She has now begun proceedings at the High Court seeking damages from the airline to help her access specialist support for her back. The BBC has contacted the airline for comment.

"When I got separated from Geoff, I knew he was in a bad way, but nothing prepared me for hearing he had died. It was absolutely devastating," she said.

Kitchen and her husband, described as her "soul mate", were starting a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia when the incident happened in May 2024.

The turbulence hit over Myanmar, with the flight then diverted to Bangkok, in Thailand, for an emergency landing.

"There had been some turbulence over Europe, and it had been shaky over the water, but it was around 10 hours into the flight when we encountered the main turbulence," Kitchen said.

"It was so severe; it felt like the aircraft was dropping. I noticed my Kindle and Geoff's phone had fallen to the floor, and I thought the plane was going down."

As the aircraft plummeted, Kitchen said her husband fell on top of her, squashing her into the armrest. Eventually, others helped to move him and a doctor on board began CPR.

Kitchen was taken to hospital while her husband was still on the plane. It was two days before she was told he had died.

It is understood that Geoff suffered a heart attack after the plane suddenly dropped at high altitude.

"I spent 10 days in hospital before I was airlifted back to Bristol. I was in so much pain that the journey was a blur. Once back in the UK, I remained in hospital for around a week and, following my discharge, required significant assistance at home," Kitchen said.

Anthe Korelidou, a specialist aviation lawyer who is representing Kitchen, said: "That Geoff was fatally injured and Linda suffered severe injuries vividly highlights the severity of what happened.

"While it's more than two years since Geoff's death, Linda and the rest of her family continue to have a number of questions and concerns about what happened and if more could have been done to prevent their injuries.

"All Linda wants is for the most thorough investigations to be conducted. The issuing of High Court proceedings is a major milestone in being able to provide Geoff's loved ones with the answers they deserve."

articles.title: Barron Trump leads reclusive life amid Iran threats, avoids public outings: Report
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump's youngest son Barron Trump, 20, has been leading a largely reclusive life amid rising security concerns and threats against.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump's youngest son Barron Trump, 20, has been leading a largely reclusive life amid rising security concerns and threats against the Trump family, according to a report by The New York Post.Barron, who recently completed his sophomore year at New York University, has spent much of the summer with his mother, First Lady Melania Trump, at Trump National Golf Club Bedminster in New Jersey.“He doesn’t go out,” a longtime Trumpworld figure told The Post, while another source described Barron as “pretty reclusive”.The 20-year-old's low profile comes after multiple assassination attempts targeting his father since July 2024.Trump was shot and wounded at a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, while another alleged gunman was arrested near his Florida golf course in September 2024.A gunman also attacked the White House Correspondents’ Dinner in April this year.Barron has also faced threats himself. Iranian hard-line media recently aired a video titled “Where to kill Barron Trump”, claiming to depict locations associated with the president's son and offering a $10 million reward for his killing, according to reports.The US Secret Service has acknowledged awareness of the video and said it investigates anything that could be perceived as a threat against its protectees.Iran's threat to BarronThe nearly three-minute video, aired by Iran's state-run broadcaster IRIB, features graphics showing places where Barron is publicly known to spend time, including Trump Tower in New York. The video also claimed that Barron's movements were being monitored and referred to a USD 10 million reward.The threat appears to be part of a broader campaign of Iranian media content targeting Trump and members of his family, according to a federal law enforcement source cited by CNN. Previous threats have also been directed at first lady Melania Trump.The White House has maintained heightened security around the Trump family following the threats. Melania Trump's office has also requested that details about Barron's private life be kept out of coverage “in light of recent threats”.Why Barron stays out of the spotlightBarron's privacy has reportedly been a longstanding preference. According to The Post, he tends to move quickly into private areas when arriving at his parents' residences and avoids spending time in public spaces.Melania Trump has also acknowledged his preference for privacy. In her documentary, she told Secret Service agents during discussions around Trump's 2025 inauguration that she knew Barron would not want to go out and said she respected his decision.Barron was reportedly also deeply affected by the 2025 assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, with whom he had become close. He was the one who informed his father about Kirk's death, according to an account cited by The Post.Experts quoted by The Post said that Barron's reclusive behaviour does not necessarily indicate trauma, but could reflect an effort to maintain privacy and make personal decisions away from public scrutiny.Barron was last seen publicly on July 19, when he accompanied his parents to watch the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina at MetLife Stadium, seated behind bulletproof glass.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Swiss gardener Jürg Wiesli grows the world’s longest chilli, measuring 52.5 cm, breaking his own Guinness World Records after nearly 8 years
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Most people who grow chillies are happy if the plant survives the summer. Jürg Wiesli wanted something else entirely. In Dozwil, a small village tucke.
articles.body: Most people who grow chillies are happy if the plant survives the summer. Jürg Wiesli wanted something else entirely. In Dozwil, a small village tucked into Switzerland's Thurgau region, he has spent years chasing one very specific goal: growing the longest chilli pepper anyone has ever measured. This summer he got there, and then some. His latest pod came in at 52.5cm, a figure that has now been confirmed by Guinness World Records and which beats a title he already held. The old record had stood for almost eight years before he broke it himself. It is a small, slightly eccentric story, but one that says a lot about patience, seed saving and a bit of stubbornness in the garden. Here is what happened, and why a pepper from a Swiss backyard has ended up making headlines around the world.A Swiss horticulturist has claimed one of the more unusual titles in the Guinness World Records book, after growing a chilli pepper long enough to rival a rolling pin. Wiesli, from Dozwil in the Swiss canton of Thurgau, has been confirmed as the grower of the longest chilli pepper ever recorded, with his prize specimen measuring an astonishing 52.5cm. According to Guinness World Records, the record was verified in Dozwil on 11 August 2026, with officials confirming the pepper as a genuine Capsicum annuum. The story has been picked up widely since, including by Moneycontrol, which reported on it under the headline "World's longest chilli ever! Swiss gardener Jürg Wiesli grows 52.5-cm pepper in Dozwil, breaks 9-year-old Guinness record".How Jürg Wiesli broke his own record for the world’s longest chilliThe interesting part is that Wiesli was not chasing someone else's title; he was chasing his own. Guinness World Records confirms his previous best for the longest chilli stood at 50.5cm, a mark that had held up for close to eight years after it was first authenticated by officials of the Great Pumpkin Commonwealth in Jona, St Gallen, Switzerland, back in September 2018.Nearly a decade between attempts gives some idea of how hard it is to push a pepper's length any further. Two centimetres might not sound like much, but in this world, where peppers are often separated by fractions of a centimetre, it is a considerable leap.How Wiesli’s saved seeds helped grow a record-breaking chilliGuinness World Records notes that this year's chilli came from the "Joe's Long" cayenne variety, a strain already popular among competitive growers for producing unusually long fruit. What set this attempt apart was the seed itself, taken not from a shop or catalogue but from Wiesli's own 48.5cm chilli grown the year before, in 2025.That habit of saving and replanting seed from his own best specimens seems to be the real trick behind his success. The strain now has its own name, the "Wiesli Big Long", a nod to years of trial, error and careful selection rather than any shortcut.How Dozwil became known for the world’s longest chilliVerification took place in Wiesli's home village, a modest municipality in Thurgau that few people outside Switzerland would recognise by name. Guinness World Records has now confirmed both the measurement and the growing method as part of the official record, putting Dozwil on the map for anyone interested in extreme vegetable growing.News of the record travelled well beyond gardening circles once it broke. Moneycontrol was among the outlets to cover it, helping bring the story to readers who would not normally follow competitive vegetable growing at all, which is often how these quirky records find their biggest audience.How Wiesli’s years-long chilli project led to a Guinness recordA 52.5cm chilli might sound like a novelty, but there is genuine skill behind it. Guinness World Records points out that record titles are updated constantly and are not always published online straight away, so serious enthusiasts tend to keep an eye on official channels rather than relying on headlines alone.For Wiesli, this is not a one-off. It is the latest step in a project that has run for years, each season's seed bringing him a little closer to the number he has now hit. Records like this rarely come from a single lucky harvest; they come from doing the same careful work, until the numbers finally move.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
